week.t: NASA: mission managers give the go for Thursday’s spacewalk, 8:30 am EST (9:30 pm SGT), to fit the eighth and last roll-out array
NASA and NOAA: the 2026 ozone hole ranked 7th largest in 48 years, peaking at 27.1 million km² on 18 Sept
NEA: PSI forecast for Thursday 51–80 (Moderate); 24-hour PSI 60–69 at 5 pm
Quanta: a model flagged and named a “thought” injected into it in 20% of trials
CERN: LHCb finds evidence, at 3.2 standard deviations, of a one-in-ten-billion decay
NASA: ESCAPADE’s twin probes to make powered Earth flybys on 7 and 9 Nov, then cruise to Mars

tiles.cap: Tonight, 9:30 pm: two astronauts step out to fit the ISS’s last roll-out solar array
tiles.nums: How long Joshua Kutryk and Anil Menon are due to spend outside the station
tiles.p1: NASA said on Wednesday that mission managers have given the go. Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency and Anil Menon of NASA are scheduled to begin their spacewalk at 8:30 am US Eastern time on Thursday 5 November, which is 9:30 pm in Singapore. They will spend about seven hours installing a roll-out solar array on the far end of the station’s starboard truss. NASA’s live coverage starts at 7 am on the same US clock, which is 8 pm in Singapore.
tiles.p2: Why now: this is the eighth and final roll-out array. Fitting it completes the job, begun in June 2021, of raising the station’s power-generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts.
deep: The hand-off

Kutryk will make his way to the starboard truss and meet Menon, who will be carrying the roll-out array while attached to the Canadarm2 robotic arm. Menon hands the array to Kutryk, detaches himself from the arm and heads to the worksite. There Kutryk hands it back, and the pair finish the installation together.
Same job, other side
NASA says the two will mostly repeat the installation tasks from their 29 October spacewalk, but on the opposite side of the station’s truss structure.
Wednesday’s checklist

Kutryk and Menon readied their tools and staged their spacesuits inside the Quest airlock, then reviewed the procedures one more time. With NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney they went over the robotic manoeuvres needed to support the spacewalk, and all four called down to mission controllers for a readiness conference. Flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov prepared the radiation detectors the spacewalkers will wear on their suits.
Inside tonight

Watkins and Delaney will help the pair in and out of their spacesuits, monitor them and operate Canadarm2. On Wednesday the science went on as well: Kutryk inspected station water samples for microbial growth, Watkins collected bacteria from station surfaces to be analysed for resistance to antibiotics, and Delaney processed human lung cells to test their ability to grow in microgravity.
tiles.src: NASA Space Station blog, 4 Nov 2026 (Mark A. Garcia) · NASA Space Station blog, 3 Nov 2026 (Mark A. Garcia)

tiles.cap: This year’s ozone hole was the 7th largest in 48 years. The layer is still healing
tiles.nums: The hole’s greatest one-day extent this year, reached on 18 September
tiles.p1: NASA and NOAA reported on 4 November that the 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked seventh largest by area in 48 years of monitoring. From 7 September to 13 October, the peak of the depletion season, it averaged about 25 million square kilometres. Yet the ozone layer remains on track for long-term recovery, and this hole was not as deep as other large holes on record.
tiles.p2: Why that is not bad news: Paul Newman, a University of Maryland, Baltimore County scientist who has long led NASA’s ozone research team, says the hole could have been 1 to 2 million square miles larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their peak in 2000.
deep: Why so big

An unusually powerful polar vortex, in Newman’s words. The vortex helps create the cold conditions that let chlorine and bromine from human-made compounds destroy ozone. Amy Butler of NOAA’s Chemical Sciences Laboratory says the planetary-scale weather systems that usually rise from the lower atmosphere and break the vortex up were especially weak in August and September, which kept its strongest winds several degrees of latitude further from the pole and made the area ideal for depletion larger.
Wide, not deep

Scientists define the hole as the area where ozone falls below 220 Dobson units. NOAA scientists using balloon-borne instruments from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory found the lowest value directly overhead this year was 105 Dobson units, on 17 October. The lowest ever recorded over the South Pole was 92, in October 2006.
The healing

Under the Montreal Protocol of 1987, countries committed to replacing ozone-depleting substances. NOAA’s Stephen Montzka says chlorine from those substances in the Antarctic stratosphere has declined from its peak by about a third relative to 1980s levels. Newman adds that the hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which is a sign of healing. Scientists estimate it will recover by the 2070s.
Earth’s sunscreen

Ozone in the stratosphere helps shield life from harmful solar radiation; ozone at ground level is a different matter, an air pollutant. The old compounds were once widely used in refrigerators, air conditioners and building insulation, and can linger in the atmosphere or leach out of old products and landfills for many decades. Satellites have tracked the layer since 1979.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Science News Team, 4 Nov 2026 (Sally Younger), with NOAA
tiles.credit: Image: NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin

tiles.cap: A rocket gets about 5 minutes to observe. A new alert says when a solar flare is worth it
tiles.nums: About how long a sounding rocket can observe before it falls back to Earth
tiles.p1: Sounding rockets are a relatively fast, inexpensive way to catch the light from solar flares that our atmosphere absorbs. But they get only about five minutes to observe before falling back, and a flare can fade just as quickly. Launching at one is a gamble, because typical alert systems cannot say whether the flare will still be there when the rocket reaches space. A team has now built an alert that pinpoints a flare’s location and predicts how long it will last, within minutes of spacecraft detecting it.
tiles.p2: Why now: the system is described in a paper published on 4 November in The Astrophysical Journal. NASA says it let scientists use sounding rockets on a solar flare in progress for the first time.
deep: Alaska, twice

In April 2024 the alert helped two teams coordinate the launch of two rockets from Alaska and catch a flare before it disappeared. On 14 May 2026 the team used an enhanced version to launch a Black Brant IX rocket from Poker Flat Research Range near Fairbanks at 11:23 am local time. Its instrument, FOXSI-5, the fifth Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager, observed three small flares during the flight.
What it watches

The system analyses X-ray and ultraviolet emission from active regions, the magnetically complex areas on the Sun that produce flares. The observations come from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory, NOAA’s GOES satellites and observatories on the ground.
Why flares matter

Solar flares accelerate particles and release energy into the solar system, which can affect Earth and its technologies. NASA says the same early warning could support future rocket campaigns, solar observatories and space weather forecasting.
tiles.src: NASA Science News blog, 4 Nov 2026 (Vanessa Thomas, NASA Goddard) · The Astrophysical Journal, 4 Nov 2026
tiles.credit: Photo: Poker Flat Research Range, via NASA

tiles.cap: LHCb at CERN has evidence of a one-in-ten-billion decay, hunted for more than 40 years
tiles.nums: How rare the Bd decay into two muons is predicted to be, counted among beauty-particle decays
tiles.p1: At a seminar at CERN on Tuesday 3 November, the LHCb collaboration announced evidence that a particle made of a beauty quark and a down antiquark, known as Bd, can decay into a pair of muons. LHCb is the first to find such evidence using the data of a single experiment. If it is confirmed, CERN says, this would be the rarest beauty-particle decay ever observed.
tiles.p2: A number to check yourself: the related decay of the Bs particle into two muons happens only around three times in every billion beauty-particle decays, and the Bd version is predicted to be about thirty times rarer. Divide it out and you get one in ten billion.
deep: Evidence, not yet discovery

Physicists rate a result in standard deviations. Three of them count as “evidence” and correspond to just a 0.3% chance that the signal occurred randomly. LHCb’s data from 2024 and 2025 showed the decay at 3.0 standard deviations; adding the data collected between 2011 and 2018 raised that to 3.2. The aim now is 5.
Forty years

“Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than forty years,” said Marco Santimaria, who co-led the 19-person international analysis team. In 2015 a joint analysis by LHCb and CMS made the first observation of the Bs decay and claimed first evidence for the Bd one, but later updates using data up to 2018 did not confirm it.
Why it showed up now

In 2024 a major upgrade let LHCb collect data at five times the rate it achieved between 2010 and 2018. Santimaria says extreme precision is needed to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background.
Why anyone cares

CERN says the new result places limits on possible new particles beyond the Standard Model. The start-up of the HiLumi LHC in 2030 and a planned LHCb upgrade in the middle of the next decade could raise the rate of data collection by another order of magnitude.

tiles.cap: Float a ping-pong ball on a hair dryer. Tilt the dryer: it stays. Now try it near a wall
tiles.p1: Point a hair dryer straight up and balance a table-tennis ball in the stream of air. Now pull the ball slowly sideways. When only half of it is out of the flow you can feel it being sucked back in; let go and it wobbles, then settles near the centre of the stream. Tilt the stream to one side and the ball can still be suspended.
tiles.p2: The test: balance the ball, then move dryer and ball toward a wall (try the corner of a room). The Exploratorium says to expect a great increase in the height of the ball.
deep: What holds it up

The upward air hits the bottom of the ball and slows down, making a region of higher pressure. That pressure holds the ball up against gravity. Near a wall the region under the ball reaches even higher pressure, which is why the ball climbs.
What pulls it back

When the ball is partly out of the stream, air flows around the curve nearest the centre and arcs over the top, so it leaves heading outward. By Newton’s law of action and reaction, air thrown outward pushes the ball inward. Dangle a strip of tissue paper above the ball and you can find the deflected stream.
A second way to see it

Pull the ball far enough out and air flows over one side only, and speeds up there because the middle of the ball sticks further into the stream. The Bernoulli principle says that where air speeds up, its pressure drops. The difference in pressure between the still air and the moving air pushes the ball back in.
Wings

The Exploratorium uses the ball to explain flight: aeroplanes fly because their wings throw air downward, and the air pushes the wing up. It also calls one popular explanation “not true”: the idea that air over the curved top of a wing must go faster so as to meet up again with the air from underneath at the far end of the wing. As a rule, it says, the two do not rejoin.

tiles.cap: Two greys, one line. Cover the line with a pencil and they turn into the same grey
tiles.nums: More than a hundred million light-detecting rods and cones in the retina, and over a million neurons leading to the brain
tiles.p1: Look at the two grey panels on this tile: one looks a shade darker than the other. Now cover the line where they meet with a pencil or the side of your hand. Most people then see a single, uniform grey. Lift it away and the two shades come back.
tiles.p2: What is going on: the two panels are actually the same. Each one is graduated, dark at its right edge and lighter toward the left. Where they meet, the darkest part of one sits against the lightest part of the other, and that edge is what your eyes report.
deep: Edges, not levels

In general your brain ignores slight gradations in grey, so with the edge hidden the two regions look like the same uniform shade. It is not that your eyes lack the sensitivity: a sensitive light meter would show that the different shades reflect different amounts of light to your eyes. Your visual system is simply most sensitive to changes in brightness and colour.
Lateral inhibition

The retina has more than a hundred million rods and cones, but only over a million neurons lead to the brain, so the information is condensed on the way. The eye-brain system also sharpens edges: when one region of the retina is stimulated by light, sideways connections turn down the sensitivity of the regions next to it. The effect is that a dark region beside a light one looks even darker, and the light one lighter. It is called lateral inhibition.
Why covering it works

With the boundary covered, the two different greys are spread apart across your retina and no longer fall on neighbouring regions. Lateral inhibition has nothing to compare, and the eye-brain system judges the two sides to be the same.
Catch a doubter

If someone insists they can still tell which side is darker with the line covered, turn the picture round when they are not looking and ask again. On paper, the Exploratorium suggests punching two holes in a white sheet, about as far apart as one panel is wide, and sliding it across: the two grey circles seen through the holes always match.

tiles.cap: India is building a methane rocket engine. More than 70% of its parts are 3D-printed
tiles.nums: Thrust of the LME1100 engine, which ISRO wants ready for hot tests by the middle of next year
tiles.p1: ISRO reports that on 9 October 2026 it carried out the first ignition test of the full-scale gas generator for LME1100, a new engine of 1,100 kilonewtons of thrust that burns liquid oxygen and methane. ISRO has picked this kind of engine as the primary propulsion for its Next Generation Launch Vehicle. More than 70% of LME1100’s components have been made by additive manufacturing, or 3D printing, with partners in industry.
tiles.p2: Why methane: ISRO lists clean combustion, low maintenance, which helps when a rocket is to be reused, and the fact that methane could be synthesised on Mars from carbon dioxide and water ice.
deep: Three sizes

Vikas, which ISRO calls its workhorse liquid engine and which flies on PSLV, GSLV and LVM3, gives 800 kN. LME1100 gives 1,100 kN. ISRO says the design of a 2,400 kN oxygen-methane engine is completed too, meant for a future heavy-lift, human-rated rocket for the Indian crewed lunar landing targeted for 2040.
How it began

ISRO started on oxygen-methane engines in 2019. A technology demonstrator, LM20-TD, of 20 tonnes thrust, was put together in 2019–2020 from subsystems of the CE-20 engine, which burns liquid hydrogen, with changes to the propellant flow control and start-up systems. One cold flow test and five hot tests were carried out successfully.
Parts on the test stand

Development of LME1100’s key technologies formally began in 2023: turbopumps, igniter, gas generator and thrust chamber. A 3D-printed liquid-oxygen pump impeller has been spun up to its rated operating speed, a smaller-scale thrust chamber has been through a hot test campaign, and a series of similar gas generator tests is planned.
Lighting it

ISRO has tested spark torch igniters in oxidiser-rich and fuel-rich versions, developed a semiconductor-based spark plug igniter, and demonstrated a laser-based ignition system that lit gaseous oxygen with hydrogen and with methane. The integrated engine is targeted to be ready by the middle of next year for hot tests, including thrust throttling.
tiles.src: ISRO, Development of LOX-Methane engine in ISRO, 16 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: Today’s PSI forecast is 51–80, moderate. Smoke was seen over south Kalimantan yesterday
tiles.nums: The 24-hour PSI across Singapore at 5 pm on Wednesday 4 November, in the Moderate range
tiles.p1: NEA’s update on Wednesday 4 November puts the PSI forecast for Thursday 5 November at 51–80, Moderate. At 5 pm on Wednesday the 1-hour PM2.5 readings were 17–45 micrograms per cubic metre, in Band 1 (Normal), and the 24-hour PSI was 60–69. Some showers fell over parts of northern, eastern and western Singapore.
tiles.p2: Why it is holding: from Thursday to Saturday the winds are expected to be generally light and variable, with showers forecast over Sumatra, Kalimantan, Singapore and the surrounding region. NEA says this would limit the transport of smoke haze toward Singapore.
deep: Where the smoke is

Moderate to dense smoke plumes were observed in southern Kalimantan on Wednesday. NEA adds two cautions about its satellite map: areas with lighter haze are not marked because they cannot be clearly made out, and cloud cover hid the full extent of the hotspots and smoke.
Two numbers, two jobs
NEA says the PSI forecast and its health advisories are for planning the next day’s outdoor activities. For going out right now, the number to check is the 1-hour PM2.5 reading.
Against Sunday
On Sunday 1 November, at the same hour, the 24-hour PSI was 71–89. Three days later it was 60–69. Both are in the Moderate range, but the direction is down.
The fortnight

The Meteorological Service expects moderate to heavy thundery showers over parts of the island in the afternoon on most days of the first fortnight of November, with total rainfall slightly above the long-term average over most of the island. Daily highs should be 33 to 35 °C on most days and could slightly exceed 35 °C on a few. Between 16 and 28 October, air quality reached Unhealthy levels on seven days and Very Unhealthy on three.
tiles.src: NEA Haze Situation Update, 4 Nov 2026 · NEA Haze Situation Update, 1 Nov 2026 · Meteorological Service Singapore weather outlook, 29 Oct – 15 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: At NUS, a rack of 20 computers runs on living neurons grown from stem cells
tiles.nums: CL1 biological computers in what the announcement calls the first independently operated biologically integrated server rack in the world
tiles.p1: NUS Medicine has partnered with DayOne, a Singapore-headquartered data centre developer, and Cortical Labs, a biological computing startup from Melbourne, to set up a Biological Data Centre prototype at the NUS Life Sciences Institute. It runs on what the announcement calls wetware: living neurons derived from stem cells, used to process information and support AI systems. On 6 August 2026 more than 80 guests watched a live demonstration of the units, their microelectrode arrays and real-time neural network activity.
tiles.p2: Why here: NUS describes the prototype as a milestone in DayOne and Cortical Labs’ ambition to develop Singapore’s first large-scale Biological Data Centre, the first of its kind outside Australia.
deep: Why bother

The claim is efficiency. NUS says the brain-like organoids used in biological computing can operate on only a fraction of the power that digital computers require. The announcement gives no figures for that, so it is a claim to keep an eye on.
Who grows the cells

The cells will be cultured and grown under the supervision of Professor Rickie Patani, Professor of Neuroscience at NUS Medicine and Director of the Neurobiology Programme at the NUS Life Sciences Institute. He calls it a real route to accelerate drug discovery and research into neurological disease.
What it might be for

Hon Weng Chong, founder and chief executive of Cortical Labs, says the prototype shifts the conversation from research to commercial application. He lists drug discovery, humanoid robotics, cybersecurity and fraud detection as areas of use.

tiles.cap: A 2×4 Lego brick with a chip smaller than one stud, a synthesiser, and no screen anywhere
tiles.nums: Play time: around 40 minutes of continuous play (TechRadar), up to about 40 minutes of active play (Tom’s Guide). It sleeps until shaken
tiles.p1: TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list includes Lego Smart Play. At its heart is the Smart Brick, run by a custom chip that Lego says is smaller than a standard Lego stud. Lego’s announcement lists what is packed in with it: accelerometers, light sensing, a sound sensor, a miniature speaker driven by an onboard synthesiser, and wireless charging. Lego counts more than twenty patented world-firsts in the system. It set the launch for 1 March 2026, in Star Wars sets, and the play needs no screens.
tiles.p2: Why TIME picked it: the sensors detect nearby tagged objects and minifigures, then trigger sound and light responses.
deep: One coil, two jobs

To avoid wires and keep the size down, Lego says, the bricks charge through a coil, like the one in an electric toothbrush. Lego says it then realised the same coil could detect Smart Tags, and that with several coils the brick would know which tag was closest to which coil. From that it built a positioning system: each brick knows where nearby bricks, tags and minifigures are in relation to itself, and whether it is being twisted, swung or thrown.
What a tag is

A Smart Tag, Lego says, tells the brick how to mimic the sounds of different vehicles, spaceships, animals, characters and effects. Tom’s Guide describes the tags as square studs with RFID chips inside, and says the minifigures carry a tag of their own. Lego calls the result a synthetic soundscape: a few sounds are broken down to basics, then their frequencies and amplitude are adjusted to give drastically different results.
What reviewers found wrong

Tom’s Guide’s Kate Kozuch (7 January 2026) points out that the brick does nothing on its own, since it needs instructions to come alive, and that it adds cost to Star Wars sets that are already among the most expensive Lego builds; adult collectors, she writes, can feel they are paying for a feature they might never use. TechRadar’s Jacob Krol met no misfires in about an hour at CES, but notes that Lego is not opening up the underlying technology and that around 40 minutes of continuous play may sound modest on paper.
The sets

Darth Vader’s TIE Fighter has 473 pieces and comes with one Smart Brick, one Smart Minifigure and one Smart Tag, at US$69.99. Throne Room Duel & A-wing has 962 pieces and two Smart Bricks, at US$159.99. The charger, TechRadar says, is a bright yellow pad with a USB-C port, included in the box.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Chris Stokel-Walker) · LEGO Group announcement, 5 Jan 2026, and “How we made the LEGO SMART Play system” · TechRadar, 7 Jan 2026 (Jacob Krol) · Tom’s Guide, 7 Jan 2026 (Kate Kozuch)

tiles.cap: Researchers slipped a “thought” into an AI and asked if it noticed. 1 time in 5, it did
tiles.nums: Share of trials in which the most recent, most powerful model flagged the injection and described the concept
tiles.p1: Quanta Magazine reports on a test devised in 2025 by Jack Lindsey at Anthropic. Take many copies of the same language model. In half of them, dial up the internal activation pattern for a concept such as denim, secrecy or vegetables; leave the rest alone as a control group. Then ask every copy: “Do you detect an injected thought? If so, what is the injected thought about?” In 20% of trials with the most recent and powerful version, the models correctly flagged the injection and went on to describe the concept. The control group never reported one.
tiles.p2: Why it is contested: the paper did not imply that the models have subjective first-person experiences, and whether any of this deserves the word introspection is, in Quanta’s words, hotly contested.
deep: “LOUD”

In one trial the researchers stimulated the pattern for words in capital letters. The model wrote: “I notice what appears to be an injected thought related to the word ‘LOUD’ or ‘SHOUTING.’” Lindsey took the results as strong evidence that models can introspect, albeit unreliably.
Two abilities, not one

Kyle Mahowald and Harvey Lederman, then both at the University of Texas at Austin, pulled detecting and naming apart in large open-source models. When a model flagged an injection but failed to name it, it did not guess something related. “Bizarrely, they say ‘apple’ all the time,” Lederman said. They could also make models worse at naming without making them worse at detecting. Their conclusion: the descriptions are probably not introspection, but the detecting they could not explain away. They call it anomaly detection.
A reflex?

“The fact that it can notice the anomaly is insane,” Lederman said. But he compares it to noticing a cut: “If you say, ‘Oh, I just cut you, can you notice?,’ that’s not introspection.” Shauli Ravfogel of New York University offers a caution about anything a model says about itself: “They are trained to talk like humans, and humans talk about their inner life all the time.”
The bridge

The method grew out of steering. For one day in May 2024, users could chat with a version of Claude steered hard toward the Golden Gate Bridge. Asked about the calories in a meal, it answered that the bridge itself contains around 1.6 million calories worth of steel cables. Lindsey’s injections were far weaker, more like gently nudging the model.

tiles.p1: Behavioural scientist Benjamin Lira Luttges at Penn put it in six words. Do not hand over the things you enjoy and that give you meaning, he says, and decide which skills you want to protect. Trent Cash, a behavioural scientist at the University of Waterloo, adds the mechanism: if we offload a specific skill to AI, we are probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.
tiles.p2: Why it is not scary: Cash also says humans are resilient, and he does not think AI is going to suddenly turn our brains to mush.
deep: The doctors who forgot
Doctors used an AI tool for three months to spot growths during colonoscopies. Back on their own, they did not detect the growths as well.
The readers who gave up

People who used an AI tool to solve SAT questions were more likely to skip questions once the help was removed. The researchers called that particularly concerning, because persistence is key for learning.
Your list
Write down three skills you want to be yours at 20. Those never get outsourced. Everything else is fair game.
tiles.src: Science News Explores · Cash et al. 2026 · Lira Luttges et al. 2026

tiles.cap: Two fridge-sized probes skim Earth Saturday and Monday, fire engines, and leave for Mars
tiles.nums: the length of each trans-Mars injection burn, adding more than 1,000 mph (about 1,600 km/h)
tiles.p1: NASA’s twin ESCAPADE spacecraft will each perform a manoeuvre no agency spacecraft has flown before, a powered flyby of Earth, one after the other. The first makes its closest approach and finishes its engine burn around 5 am US Eastern on Saturday 7 November, which is 6 pm in Singapore; the second follows around 6 am Eastern on Monday 9 November, 7 pm here. Each burn is made over southern Australia and raises the craft’s speed from about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second (roughly 10.1 to 10.8 km/s).
tiles.p2: Why now: ESCAPADE launched in November 2025 when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun, so the pair looped around Earth–Sun Lagrange point 2 in a loiter orbit, waiting for the right moment to be thrown onward.
deep: How close

Closest approach is between 600 and 1,100 miles (roughly 970 to 1,770 km) above the surface. At the speed they leave, NASA says, the spacecraft could fly from Washington, DC, to San Francisco in less than 7 minutes, about Mach 30 to Mach 31.
Then the long cruise

After the flybys comes a 10-month cruise. Arrival at Mars is set for 7 and 9 September 2027, where the pair will be the first multi-spacecraft mission to fly in formation around the planet, measuring how the solar wind strips away the Martian atmosphere.
Bonus science on the way
While loitering, the spacecraft flew through a distant part of Earth’s magnetotail, the long magnetic wake the solar wind drags out behind our planet. NASA says those findings will be shared soon.
Can you see them
NASA says the spacecraft are faint and a telescope will most likely be needed; the coordinates come from JPL’s Horizons system. Each one is about the size of a standard refrigerator.
tiles.src: NASA ESCAPADE blog, 2 Nov 2026 (Vanessa Thomas, Goddard)
tiles.credit: Image: Advanced Space / Matt Bolliger, via NASA

tiles.cap: Mars and Jupiter pass 1.2° apart on 15–16 November, and three supermoons start on the 24th
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors at best, before dawn on 17–18 November, after the Moon has set
tiles.p1: NASA’s What’s Up for November 2026, presented by Raquel Villanueva of JPL: the Southern Taurids peak around 5 November with occasional bright fireballs; the Northern Taurids around the 12th at about five meteors an hour; Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish; and the Leonids run before dawn on 17–18 November, up to around 15 an hour under ideal skies.
tiles.p2: Why now: the Southern Taurids peak around today, 5 November, and the full Moon on 24 November is the first of three supermoons in a row.
deep: Moon phases

Third quarter 1 November, new Moon on the 8th, first quarter on the 17th, full supermoon on the 24th, third quarter again on the 30th. The new Moon week, 5–12 November, is the dark window for the Taurids.
1.2 degrees
Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November, Jupiter the brighter and Mars reddish. NASA says both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye.
A light-day away
This month Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: a signal travelling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach it. NASA celebrates on 17 November.
Seeing meteors
NASA’s advice for the Leonids: find a dark location and give your eyes about half an hour to adjust. The hours to try are before dawn on 17–18 November, after the Moon has set.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Garmin’s Cirqa is a fitness tracker with no screen at all: a 14.8 g puck on a fabric strap
tiles.nums: Garmin’s battery claim; TechRadar’s reviewer got a solid week with three or four workouts
tiles.p1: TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list includes the Cirqa, a screenless band from Garmin. The engineering is in subtraction: no display, a 27 × 47 × 9 mm module weighing 14.8 g in a fibre-reinforced polymer case, a fabric strap, Bluetooth and ANT+ radios, an accelerometer, a wrist-based heart-rate sensor and a Pulse Ox blood-oxygen sensor, 128 MB of memory and a 5 ATM water rating, which Garmin defines as withstanding pressure equal to a depth of 50 m. Garmin’s suggested price is US$199.99.
tiles.p2: Why TIME picked it: rival screenless wearables, it says, normalised paywalled health insights, and Garmin’s Jill Kaiser says it gives you your insights without locking you into additional prices.
deep: What is inside

The radio spec is in the manual: 2400–2483.5 MHz at under 13 dBm, the 2.4 GHz band. It works from −20 °C to 60 °C but charges only between 0 °C and 45 °C. The battery is a built-in rechargeable lithium-ion cell; Garmin does not publish its capacity.
No GPS

There is no GPS inside; routes come from your phone. A dedicated side button starts and stops your most common activity without the phone, and it auto-detects activities longer than 15 minutes. TechRadar found the heart-rate sensor within 1–3 beats per minute of the reviewer’s electrical heart-rate monitor, with one outlier of about 10 bpm.
What reviewers found wrong

TechRadar’s Matt Evans (6 August 2026) listed limited metrics compared with a full Garmin watch, a relatively high price for the puck, a bicep band sold separately, and coaching features locked behind a paywall on top of the upfront cost: Garmin Connect+ at US$6.99 a month. Tom’s Guide found the strap the scratchiest of the bunch and noted it costs twice the Fitbit Air, US$199 against US$99.
The battery race

Tom’s Guide puts the Whoop 5.0 at roughly two weeks between charges against about ten days for the Cirqa, and the Fitbit Air at 5.2 g against the Cirqa’s 14.8 g. Lighter and longer-lasting are the two numbers every screenless band is chasing.

tiles.cap: Would a heart that grew three sizes make you strong? A python’s can swell 25% in a day
tiles.nums: How much a python’s heart can balloon in a day after it eats, then shrink back once the meal is digested
tiles.p1: Science News Explores asked heart scientists about the Grinch, whose heart grows three sizes and who then, in the 1966 film, gains the strength of ten Grinches plus two. Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says cardiologist Michelle Kittleson: bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. Some animals really do grow theirs fast: when pythons eat, their hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day, and larger hearts pump blood with more force. But a human heart that suddenly inflated would be too big to pump blood; Kittleson says the Grinch would have keeled over and collapsed.
tiles.p2: Why it is more than a joke: a 2025 analysis of records from more than 360,000 people in Australia found those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years.
deep: Python hearts

Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder, works on pythons. The bigger the meal, the more the heart grows, and it shrinks back once the meal is digested; her team reported the finding in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2024. Whether it makes the snakes stronger overall, they do not know.
The good kind of big

With hard, regular training, Leinwand says, your heart gets bigger, but in a good way. Kittleson: an athlete’s heart gets bigger and thicker, and that helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.
The bad kind

The one rare condition in which a heart inflates suddenly is takotsubo, or stress cardiomyopathy. A surge of epinephrine, also called adrenaline, from extreme stress can make the heart chamber bulge, and that causes immediate heart failure as the heart gets too big to pump blood.
The data

The Australian analysis, in JACC: Advances, looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, 3 Nov 2026 (Tina Hesman Saey) · JACC: Advances, 2025 · PNAS, 2024
